reason: While the text does depict conflict at the national level between the Egyptian people and the Hebrew/Israelite people, the statement is contradicted by the text's explicit religious framing. The conflict is repeatedly positioned as a demonstration of divine power—'that you may know that I am the Lord your God' (לְמַעַן תֵּדַע כִּי־ אֵין כַּיהוָה אֱלֹהֵינוּ) and 'that I am the Lord in the midst of the land' (כִּי אֲנִי יְהוָה בְּקֶרֶב הָאָרֶץ). The request to 'let my people go to serve me' (שַׁלַּח עַמִּי וְיַֽעַבְדֻֽנִי) is explicitly religious. Additionally, there is a personal dimension: Pharaoh is directly addressed and his heart is hardened by God through divine action. The conflict is multivalent—simultaneously national (peoples and lands), religious (God's authority and worship), and personal (Pharaoh as protagonist).
